strengths: Novel and well-motivated focus: shifting cultural evaluation of T2I models from object-centric artifacts to social activities, which are contextual and compositional and expose distinct failure modes (wrong activity, hallucinated elements, exaggeration).

Substantial benchmark construction effort: 576 prompts across 16 countries and 9 activity categories, 19,000+ generated images from 6 modern T2I models (including recent proprietary ones like GPT-Image-1 and Nano-Banana), plus ~3k real reference images.

Explainable descriptor-based metric suite (ALIGN, HAL, EXAG, DDIV, SDIV) that provides interpretable, multi-level feedback rather than opaque scores, grounded in a reasonable proposer-refiner descriptor pipeline with an ablation (Table 3) showing it improves quality.

Careful human evaluation protocol: nationality/ residence-verified Prolific annotators, attention checks, repeated questions, free-text rationales, and follow-up discussions; human-human agreement is reported for calibration.

Useful empirical findings: consistent Global North vs. Global South gaps (4-8% alignment) across all six models, and a clear demonstration that prior image-text alignment metrics correlate poorly (sometimes negatively) with human judgments on cultural faithfulness, plus per-dimension and per-country analyses.

Thoughtful methodology details: threshold τ calibrated on real (not synthetic) images to avoid leakage, with ablations over quartile choices (Table 4); descriptor accuracy validated by humans (90.27%); limitations section candidly discusses LLM cultural bias.
weaknesses: Absolute correlation with human judgment is modest: FAITH achieves Spearman ~0.33-0.38 vs. human-human agreement of only 0.42, so much of the achievable ceiling remains unexplained; the '7% better' headline gain is incremental and statistical significance of the correlation improvements is not reported.

Potential circularity in the bias argument: the paper criticizes VLM-based metrics for inheriting Western-centric bias, yet its own ground-truth descriptors are generated by GPT-4o/Gemini (web-trained LLMs) and extracted from images using InternVL (a VLM); the mitigation via proposer-refiner is empirical but does not eliminate the concern that the reference standard encodes the same biases it aims to detect.

Human validation coverage is limited: only 7 countries, 3 public models, and 216 total evaluation forms; no human validation of the diversity metrics (DDIV/SDIV), so half of the proposed metric suite is essentially unvalidated.

The real reference images (Google search with CLIPScore filtering, 5 per prompt) are noisy and potentially stereotyped themselves; EXAG is defined relative to these references (Eq. 3-4), and Table 10 shows the EXAG variant choices materially affect results (some even negatively correlated), suggesting fragility.
Unfair comparison conditions in Table 1: proprietary models generate only N=1 image per prompt versus N=10 for public models, complicating cross-model faithfulness conclusions.
The composite FAITH score is an ad hoc arithmetic mean of rescaled components; no justification or alternative aggregations are explored.

Benchmark construction relies heavily on GPT-4o parsing CulturalAtlas and Wikipedia, which may skew coverage toward well-documented (often Western or globally famous) activities, potentially confounding the Global North/South analysis.
Classification into Global North (5 countries) vs. Global South (11 countries) is imbalanced, and country-level conclusions (e.g., China performing strongly) are not deeply analyzed.
Writing has notable typos/incomplete sentences (e.g., 'included mistakenly ,', 'diversity metric do not provide insights', truncated EXAG analysis in appendix), which detract from polish.

strengths: The paper targets an underexplored and meaningful problem: cultural faithfulness of T2I models for social activities, which is compositional and contextual in a way that prior object-centric benchmarks (food, attire, landmarks) are not.
The benchmark is reasonably large in scale: 576 prompts, 16 countries, 9 activity categories, 6 T2I models, and 19k+ generated images, with real reference images collected and filtered.

A controlled human study on Prolific with reasonable quality controls (attention checks, repeated questions, free-text rationales, native annotator recruitment) provides ground-truth labels for metric validation.
The finding that image-text alignment metrics correlate poorly (or even positively) with cultural exaggeration is an interesting and useful diagnostic observation for the community.
The proposed metrics provide interpretable, descriptor-level feedback (top/bottom-k missing or exaggerated descriptors), which is more actionable than opaque alignment scores.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in methodology. The core machinery is a straightforward combination of existing ideas: LLM-generated descriptors (Menon & Vondrick, 2023), self-consistency-style proposer-refiner prompting (Wang et al., 2022), and sentence-embedding matching. The claimed contribution is primarily a new benchmark plus a thin wrapper of metrics rather than a substantive technical advance.

The headline gain over baselines is modest and brittle. FAITH achieves Spearman 0.38 overall versus 0.42 human-human agreement; the claimed '7% better' correlation is small in absolute terms, and per-model results (Table 8) are unstable (e.g., ALIGN 0.397 on Flux1 but only 0.208 on Qwen). No statistical significance tests are reported for any of the correlations or GN/GS gaps.

The evaluation itself is circular and potentially biased. The pipeline relies on GPT-4o/Gemini to generate descriptors and InternVL to extract descriptors from images, yet the paper's central criticism is that LLM/VLM internal knowledge inherits Western-centric bias. The ablation showing EXAG with LLM GT descriptors yields negative correlation (-0.25, Table 10) suggests the approach is highly sensitive to the choice of descriptor source, and the paper does not convincingly demonstrate its pipeline escapes the bias it criticizes.

Human evaluation is small relative to the claims: 216 forms covering only 7 of 16 countries, 9 activities per country, and 3 of the 6 models. Descriptor accuracy (90.27%) is validated on this same small subset, so generalization of the metrics to the full benchmark is unverified.

Metric definitions are ad hoc. Exaggeration is defined as a max over image-text alignment differences against real references collected via Google search and CLIPScore filtering, a noisy reference set that the paper itself admits is biased; the faithfulness score is a plain arithmetic mean with no theoretical or empirical justification of the aggregation. Threshold tau selection is a percentile heuristic with modest ablations.

Experimental setup inconsistencies undermine confidence: proprietary models use only N=1 image, making their alignment/diversity scores incomparable to the N=10 public models in Table 1; the GN/GS split is unbalanced (5 vs 11 countries); China is noted as an outlier in Fig. 3a but not analyzed.

The paper is not ready for publication in its current form: duplicated and incorrect table/figure captions in the appendix (e.g., 'EXAG can effectively detect hallucinations', 'ALIGN Likert Scoring Prompt' used for HAL and EXAG), broken sentences (Sec. 5.2 'we do not human annotators a related question'), a table listing a nonexistent 'Soft Score' description, and inconsistent benchmark naming (CULTIVate vs CULTIVateBench).

Reproducibility concerns: results depend on proprietary, non-versioned APIs (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DALL-E 3, GPT-Image-1, Nano-Banana) for both descriptor generation and model evaluation, and no release of code or the benchmark is stated.

The Global North bias finding, while plausibly true, is largely confirmatory of prior work (Bayramli et al., ViSAGe, Culture-TRIP, etc.), and the paper's positioning relative to the concurrent CuRe and Nayak et al. work is not sufficiently differentiated beyond the activity-vs-object framing.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: shifting cultural evaluation of T2I models from object-centric artifacts to contextual, compositional social activities is a meaningful gap, and the paper argues convincingly (e.g., the 'elephant ant man game' example) why existing alignment metrics are unsuitable for this setting.

Substantial benchmark construction: 576 prompts across 16 countries and 9 activity categories, 19k+ generated images, and ~3k filtered real reference images; the systematic pipeline (CulturalAtlas + Wikipedia parsing with GPT-4o) is documented and reproducible.

The AHEaD framework (Alignment, Hallucination, Exaggeration, Diversity) is interpretable and decomposes failure modes in a way prior VLM-based metrics cannot; the proposer-refiner descriptor pipeline with human validation (90.27% descriptor accuracy) is a sensible quality control, with ablations showing it helps (Table 3).

The headline negative finding — image-text alignment metrics correlate positively with cultural exaggeration while they should correlate negatively — is an interesting and useful diagnostic result for the community.

Real human study with domain-matched annotators (nationality/residence verification), attention checks, consistency tests, free-text rationales, and direct discussion; this is more careful quality control than typical for such studies.

Clear empirical takeaway (systematic Global North > Global South gap of 4-8% alignment across all six T2I models) plus per-dimension failure analysis (Fig. 4) and metric correlation analysis (Fig. 5).
Good reproducibility: seeds specified, models and versions named, full prompts included in the appendix, threshold calibration procedure described.
weaknesses: The human validation of the metrics is narrow relative to the benchmark's scale: only 7 of 16 countries, only 3 public models, and 189 evaluation forms. The central claim that AHEaD 'achieves 7% better correlation with human judgment' rests on this small subset, and absolute correlations remain moderate (FAITH 0.38 vs. human-human 0.42), leaving substantial room for doubt about the metrics' reliability.

There is a circularity tension the paper criticizes in others but only partially escapes: the 'ground truth' descriptors come from LLMs (GPT-4o/Gemini) whose cultural knowledge is itself Western-biased. The proposer-refiner mitigates but does not eliminate this, and the Limitations section acknowledges it without quantifying the residual bias impact on GS countries.

The hallucination metric defined purely by embedding-similarity thresholding against LLM descriptors is fragile for exactly the phenomenon the paper emphasizes — multiple valid cultural variants — and depends on a sensitive threshold τ (Table 4 shows large swings: 0.21 to 0.33 across quantiles).

Exaggeration depends on CLIPScore-filtered web images (top-5 of 20), introducing reference bias and noise that the paper itself concedes ('noisy ground-truth images'); the Diversity metrics are not validated against human judgment at all.

Unfair comparison conditions between proprietary (N=1) and public models (N=10) complicate the cross-model conclusions in Table 1, and the paper does not disentangle the effect of N from model quality.

Presentation issues: several appendix tables have leftover/incorrect labels (e.g., two tables titled 'ALIGN Likert Scoring Prompt' where one is HAL; Table 7 heading says 'EXAG can effectively detect hallucinations'; Table 6 caption references an undefined 'Soft Score'); typos ('achieves 7%' framing, 'metric achieves' sentence fragments) suggest insufficient proofreading.

The GN/GS dichotomy (5 vs. 11 countries) is coarse; the observation that models perform strongly on China is flagged but not analyzed, and country-level sample sizes are small enough that per-country rankings (Fig. 4) may be unstable.

The 'first work to use descriptors for evaluating cultural competence in T2I models' claim needs softening given the density of concurrent cultural-evaluation work (CuRe, CulturalFrames, Geodiv) and the reliance on established descriptor-generation ideas (Menon & Vondrick, CuPL-style).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated angle: shifting cultural evaluation of T2I models from object-centric artifacts to social activities, which are compositional and contextual. The distinction between faithfulness and diversity, and between alignment, hallucination, and exaggeration, is conceptually clear and practically useful.

Substantial empirical effort: CULTIVate spans 16 countries, 576 activities across 9 categories, 19,000+ generated images from 6 recent T2I models (including proprietary ones), and ~3k real reference images, providing a reusable community resource.

The AHEaD framework is a sensible design: using MLLMs only for generic scene understanding (descriptor extraction) rather than direct cultural scoring, and comparing against LLM-generated reference descriptors, mitigates some concerns about VLM cultural bias while retaining interpretability.

Stronger validation than most cultural benchmarking papers: human study with native-annotator matching per country, attention checks, free-text rationales, Krippendorff's Alpha reported and benchmarked against prior work, and threshold τ calibrated on real images rather than synthetic ones to avoid leakage.

Useful and actionable findings: systematic Global North vs. Global South bias, ITA metrics correlating (even positively) with exaggeration, per-country and per-activity analysis, and a preliminary demonstration that descriptor-level feedback supports targeted image editing.
Ablations (proposer-refiner vs. proposer-only, threshold selection, descriptor source for EXAG) support individual design choices, and correlations are reported with statistical significance.
weaknesses: Absolute correlation with human judgment remains moderate: FAITH achieves ~0.42-0.47 Spearman vs. ~0.58 human-human correlation. The headline '27% higher correlation' is relative, and the metric still explains well under half the variance in human judgments, so the metric is a noisy proxy.

Circularity/bias concerns in the evaluation stack: reference descriptors come from GPT-4o/Gemini, predicted descriptors from InternVL3/Qwen2.5-VL, similarity from sentence embeddings, and EXAG relies on VQAScore (an ITA metric the paper itself criticizes). LLM-generated descriptors may encode the same WEIRD biases the paper documents, and 'hallucination' risks penalizing legitimate cultural variants absent from the reference set.

The human study is relatively small and limited: 398 forms / 796 annotations, only 3 public T2I models and real images for 3 countries; proprietary models evaluated with a single image per prompt, raising variance concerns for Table 1 GN/GS conclusions. Inter-rater agreement ranges from 0.15 to 0.62 (low in some countries).

The diversity metrics (DDIV, SDIV) are defined but not clearly validated against human judgments, unlike the faithfulness components; their correlation with human perceptions of variety is not established.

Several presentation issues: duplicated sentences in Sec. 4.2 (descriptor quality measures repeated verbatim), typos in Table 1 (e.g., ±0.3, missing error values for FAITH), hard-to-read figures (Fig. 3b, Fig. 4), and inconsistent naming (AHEAD/AHEaD).

EXAG's definition depends on LLM-proposed stereotype candidates, which risks reifying stereotypes as the reference notion of 'exaggeration'; the ablation (Table 10) shows weak average correlation (~0.18) for the adopted ITA-based EXAG, and the MLLM-based variant that correlates better is set aside for interpretability reasons.

Positioning against concurrent work (Nayak et al., 2025) is acknowledged but not deeply compared experimentally, so the claim of being the 'first automated metrics for social activities' is difficult to verify.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored dimension of cultural evaluation: social activities (dining, greeting, dancing, games) rather than static object-centric artifacts, and the motivation that activities are compositional and contextual is well argued.
CULTIVate is a substantial benchmarking effort: 576 activities across 9 categories, 16 countries, 19,000+ generated images from 6 recent T2I models, plus ~3,000 real reference images.

The AHEaD decomposition (Alignment / Hallucination / Exaggeration / Diversity) is a sensible diagnostic framing, and the finding that ITA metrics correlate positively with exaggeration (rewarding stereotypes) is an interesting and useful negative result.

The human study uses nationality-verified annotators, per-country Likert labels for faithfulness/hallucination/exaggeration, attention checks, and reports Krippendorff's Alpha comparable to prior cross-cultural work.

The analysis of Global North vs. Global South disparities is consistent across models and corroborated by both automatic metrics and raw human scores (Table 13), which strengthens the main empirical finding.
weaknesses: Circularity / borrowed bias: the reference descriptors are LLM-generated (GPT-4o as refiner) and the predicted descriptors are extracted by MLLMs. The paper criticizes VLMs/LLMs for WEIRD cultural bias, yet the entire evaluation apparatus rests on exactly those biased models. The Proposer-Refiner mitigates this only weakly (90% precision on 378 descriptors is a thin validation), and the limitations section acknowledges the problem without resolving it.

The headline claims are overstated. The '27% higher correlation' is a relative improvement over a weak same-backbone MLLM-as-judge baseline (0.47 vs 0.20 absolute Spearman). More damaging, the GPT-4o MLLM-as-judge baseline achieves 0.48 vs FAITH's 0.47 (Table 2) and 0.43 average per-model correlation vs ALIGN's 0.38 (Table 6) — a simple GPT-4o judge essentially matches the proposed multi-component framework, which undercuts the central contribution.

Absolute agreement with humans is modest: best metric correlation ~0.47 against a human-human correlation of 0.58, with moderate inter-rater agreement (Alpha 0.15-0.62) on a small human study (398 forms, 11 of 16 countries, only 3 T2I models). The validation set is too limited to firmly establish metric validity.

The real-image reference pipeline (Google search + CLIPScore top-5 filtering) likely reinforces exactly the stereotypical depictions the paper is trying to measure, and these same images are used for threshold calibration (tau), EXAG baselines, and annotation — raising contamination and bias-reinforcement concerns that are not analyzed.

Unfair model comparison: proprietary models get 1 image per prompt vs 10 for public models, yet all models are ranked together in Table 1 and the GN/GS conclusions; the effect of N on ALIGN/HAL estimates is not controlled for proprietary systems.

Descriptor-guided image editing (Fig. 8) is purely qualitative and admittedly preliminary; no quantitative before/after evaluation is provided, so the claimed practical utility of interpretable feedback remains unvalidated.

FAITH is a simple arithmetic mean of ALIGN, 1-HAL, 1-EXAG with no weighting justification, sensitivity analysis, or comparison to alternative aggregations; and EXAG is dropped or weakly validated in parts (Table 9-10 show ITA-based EXAG correlation of only 0.18-0.29, and the adopted variant is worse than the MLLM variant).

Significant writing and presentation issues that should not appear at this stage: duplicated verbatim text in Sec. 4.2 (the two recall-estimation measures are repeated word-for-word), inconsistent naming (AHEaD vs AHEAD vs AHFaD), 'Human evaluation showed 90%.' as a sentence fragment, broken uncertainty values (0.12 ±0.3), a sentence in the conclusion ending with a comma ('Global South. and demonstrate'), garbled references ('wcountries', 'Table.32'), and Fig. 5a referenced before the corresponding discussion exists.

Positioning against concurrent work (Nayak et al., 2025 CulturalFrames) is thin; the descriptor-generation idea is a direct extension of Menon & Vondrick (2023) to a new domain, limiting methodological novelty.

Several important details are under-specified in the main text: how the five dimensions are aggregated, how the refiner deduplicates across heterogeneous LLM outputs, and how the 9 activity categories and 16 countries were balanced — the reader must rely on appendix fragments.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely understudied and important problem: evaluating cultural faithfulness of T2I models through social activities rather than object-centric artifacts. The motivation is well-grounded (activities are compositional and contextual, so ITA metrics fail differently here).

CULTIVate is a substantial benchmark: 576 activities across 16 countries and 9 categories, 19,000+ generated images, 3,000 real reference images, covering 6 recent T2I models including both public and proprietary systems.

The AHEaD framework is well-motivated and interpretable. The decomposition into Alignment, Hallucination, Exaggeration, and Diversity, and the finding that ITA metrics positively correlate with exaggeration (i.e., reward stereotypical elements), is an insightful and practically relevant analysis that will matter to practitioners.

The proposer-refiner descriptor generation pipeline is a sensible approach to scalable reference construction, and it is validated via human annotation (90% precision, 4.5/5 coverage rating), with ablations (Table 4) showing it improves over proposer-only.

The human study is well designed: country-matched native annotators via Prolific, attention checks, consistency checks, required rationales, and inter-rater agreement (Krippendorff's Alpha) reported and compared against prior cross-cultural work.

Reproducibility support is good: prompts are provided in the appendix, model/backbone choices and thresholds are specified, and calibration of tau on real images (to avoid leakage from synthetic data) is a thoughtful detail.
The GN vs. GS disparity finding (4-8% alignment gap) is consistent across all six models and corroborated by human scores (Table 13), giving it credibility.
weaknesses: Absolute metric quality is moderate: FAITH achieves Spearman correlations of only 0.42-0.47 with human faithfulness judgments, against a human-human ceiling of 0.58. The headline '27% higher correlation' is a relative improvement over weak baselines, so claims like 'enables iterative image refinement' overstate what the evidence supports; the framework still fails to explain over half the variance in human judgment.

Potential circularity between LLM-generated reference descriptors and the models under evaluation: reference descriptors come from GPT-4o/Gemini trained on similar web data as T2I models, so the metric may inherit and re-encode the same WEIRD/cultural biases it aims to measure. The limitations section acknowledges this but does not empirically control for it.

The GN-vs-GS gap could partly be an artifact of descriptor quality differences (LLMs likely produce better and richer descriptors for GN countries), rather than purely a property of the T2I models. No experiment disentangles these two confounds.

The human validation covers only a subset of the benchmark: 11 of 16 countries, 3 of 6 T2I models (public only), 1-2 activities per category, and 398 forms. Several key results (e.g., metric correlations) are therefore validated on a limited slice of the benchmark.

The Exaggeration component is the weakest link: EXAG correlations with human judgment are low (0.25-0.34), and the authors adopt the ITA-based EXAG variant in FAITH despite their own Table 9 showing the MLLM-based variant correlates better with GT-EXAG. This design choice (justified only by interpretability) undermines the composite metric.

Proprietary models are evaluated with only 1 image per prompt (no seeds), so N=1/N=10 comparisons and diversity metrics are unavailable for DALL-E 3, GPT-Image-1, and Gemini, weakening cross-model comparisons.

Presentation and writing issues reduce polish: duplicated sentences in Sec 4.2, grammatical errors ('achieves highest correlation than'), ambiguous error notation ('+-'), inconsistent table formatting (e.g., '0.12 +- 0.3' in Table 1), and duplicated content between Sec 4.2 and Appendix A.5 regarding descriptor recall estimation.

Statistical significance is reported for metric correlations but not for the GN-GS disparity claims, and per-country inter-rater agreement varies widely (0.15-0.62), which places nontrivial uncertainty on the headline findings for low-agreement countries.

Descriptor-guided image editing (Fig. 8) is only a preliminary, qualitative demonstration on 4 activities with no quantitative evaluation, yet it is used to support capability claims in the abstract and contributions.
